sentences.text: Understanding the events leading up to Salamis, the strategies employed, and the key figures involved provides valuable insight into this epic conflict .
The Battle of Salamis (September 480 BCE) remains one of the most consequential naval engagements in history.
It was the turning point of the Second Persian Invasion, where a vastly outnumbered Greek fleet utilized geography and deception to shatter the naval supremacy of King Xerxes I.

The Strategic Prelude:
After the Greek defeat at Thermopylae and the subsequent burning of Athens, the Allied Greek navy retreated to the Saronic Gulf.
While many Peloponnesian leaders wanted to retreat further to the Isthmus of Corinth, the Athenian general Themistocles argued that fighting in the narrow straits of Salamis was their only hope.
Themistocles famously forced the hand of both his allies and the Persians by sending a "traitorous" message to Xerxes via his slave, Sicinnus.
The message claimed the Greeks were panicking and intended to flee under the cover of night.
Xerxes, eager for a decisive victory, took the bait.

The Deployment:
The Persian fleet, numbering roughly 600–800 ships, moved into position overnight to block both exits of the Salamis straits, effectively trapping the Greeks.
The Persian Line: Composed of Phoenicians (right wing), Egyptians, and Ionian Greeks (left wing).
The Greek Line: Numbering roughly 370 triremes, the Athenians held the left wing (facing the Phoenicians), while the Spartans and Aeginetans held the right.

The Opening Maneuvers:
As dawn broke, the Persians advanced into the narrow channel.
This was exactly what Themistocles wanted.
In the open sea, the faster, more numerous Persian ships would have easily outflanked the Greeks.
In the straits, the Persians' numbers became a liability.
The Greeks initially backed their oars, drawing the Persians deeper into the funnel-like passage.
As the Persian front line pushed forward, the ships behind them became crowded and disorganized.

The Engagement: Chaos in the Straits:
The battle became a massive, disorganized melee.
The primary weapon was the bronze-sheathed ram at the prow of the trireme.
Collisions: Because the water was so cramped, Persian ships began to collide with one another.
When they tried to retreat, they crashed into their own reinforcements pushing forward from the rear.
The Boarding Actions: Greek triremes carried heavily armed hoplites.
Once a ship was rammed or fouled, the Greeks would board and engage in hand-to-hand combat.
The Persians, many of whom could not swim, faced certain death if their ships sank.
The Turning Point: The Athenian wing broke the Phoenician line on the Persian right.
As the Phoenicians fled, they caused a chain reaction of panic across the Persian fleet.

The Persian Retreat and Aftermath:
Watching the disaster from a golden throne on the slopes of Mount Aegaleos, Xerxes saw his elite navy decimated.
The Queen of Halicarnassus, Artemisia, famously escaped by ramming one of her own allied ships to trick the Greeks into thinking she was on their side.
By evening, the Persians had lost approximately 200 ships, while the Greeks lost only 40.

Consequences:
Persian Withdrawal: Fearing the Greeks would destroy the Hellespont bridges and trap him in Europe, Xerxes retreated to Asia with the bulk of his army.
Mardonius Remains: He left a smaller force under General Mardonius, which was eventually defeated the following year at the Battle of Plataea.
Rise of Athens: The victory solidified Athens as a premier naval power, leading directly to its "Golden Age" and the formation of the Delian League.
Did you know?
The Greek victory was also a victory for democracy.
Since the triremes required thousands of lower-class citizens (the thetes) to row, their contribution to the war effort significantly increased their political leverage in Athenian society.
The Battle of Salamis holds immense strategic significance.
The Greeks, though outnumbered, possessed a crucial advantage: their knowledge of the narrow straits of Salamis.

The Greek commander Themistocles lured the Persian fleet into this confined space, negating their numerical superiority and allowing the smaller, more maneuverable Greek ships to inflict heavy damage.
Key figures like Themistocles and Xerxes I played instrumental roles in the battle.
Themistocles, the Athenian general, masterminded the Greek strategy, while Xerxes I, the Persian king, sought to crush the Greek resistance and expand his empire.
The clash between these two leaders and their respective forces determined the fate of Greece and the future of the Western world.
The Battle of Marathon in 490 B.C. was part of the first Persian invasion of Greece.
The battle was fought on the Marathon plain of northeastern Attica and marked the first blows of the Greco-Persian War.
With the Persians closing in on the Greek capital, Athenian general Miltiades took command of the hastily assembled army.
Miltiades weakened the center of his outnumbered force to strengthen its wings, causing confusion among the invading Persians.
His strategy was victorious over the Persians’ strength, and the victory of “the Marathon men” captured the collective imagination of the Greeks.
The tale of the messenger Pheidippides running 25 miles to Athens to deliver the news of the Persian defeat inspired the creation of the modern marathon.
The Battle of Marathon was fought because the Persian Army wanted to defeat the Greek city-states that supported the uprisings in Ionia, part of modern-day Turkey, against the Persian Empire.
The first encounter on the Greek mainland between East (Persia) and West (Greece) took place in August or September of 490 B.C., on the small seaside plain of Marathon, 26 miles northeast of Athens.
The Persian expeditionary force of Darius I was not large, perhaps numbering under 30,000.
Led by generals Hippias, Datis and Artaphernes, the Persian Army arrived confident after storming the nearby Greek city-state of Eretria.
No allies except the Plataeans joined the Athenian resistance of less than 10,000 troops, and some autocratic regimes in Attica supported the invaders in the hope of toppling the fledgling democracy.
What Happened at the Battle of Marathon?

To meet the larger invading force, the Athenian army commander Miltiades thinned out his army's center and reinforced the wings, hoping that his hoplites—heavily armed foot soldiers—could hold the middle while his flanks broke through the lighter-clad Persian infantry.
In fact, the Athenian center broke, but it held long enough for the Athenians to rout the Persian wings and meet in the rear, causing a general panic among the invaders.
The Persians would invade Greece again in 480 B.C. under Xerxes I, son of Darius, who planned to succeed in conquering Greece where his father had failed.

The allied Greek city-states under King Leonidas of Sparta held off the Persian invasion for seven days in the Battle of Thermopylae, earning them a place in history for their last stand in defense of their native soil.
But it was the initial victory of the Athenians at the Battle of Marathon that is most remembered today.
Almost immediately, the victory of “the Marathon men” captured the collective imagination of the Greeks.
Ceremonial funeral mounds of the legendary 192 Athenian dead and the loyal Plataeans were erected on the battlefield.
Epigrams were composed and panoramic murals were put on display.
Most of what we know about the Battle of Marathon comes from the account of the historian Herodotus, who wrote about it around 50 years after the battle took place in his Histories.
Another famous author to immortalize the Battle was Robert Browning, who wrote the poem “Pheidippides” in 1879 to commemorate the soldier’s run from Marathon to Athens.
The first organized marathon was part of the first modern Olympics in 1896.
The ancient games, held from approximately 776 B.C. to 393 A.D., did not include the race.
Michael Bréal, a friend of modern Olympics founder Pierre de Coubertin, was inspired by the legend of the Battle of Marathon to create an endurance race.
The first marathon was 40 kilometers, or under 25 miles (as opposed to today’s 26.2 miles), and almost half of the competitors had to quit from exhaustion.
The winner of the first marathon was Spiridon Louis, a Greek shepherd who never ran another competitive race again.
The journey of Pheidippides from Marathon to Athens also inspired the first Boston Marathon on April 19, 1897.
The Boston Marathon is the world’s oldest annual marathon and is also notable for allowing women to compete in 1972 when the first Olympic marathon for women wasn’t held until 1984.
Franz Ferdinand, aged 51, was heir to the Austro-Hungarian Empire.
He was married to Sophie Chotek von Chotvoka and had three children.
Franz Ferdinand was, however, very unpopular because he had made it clear that once he became Emperor he would make changes.
This map, of the Austro-Hungarian Empire in 1914, shows that Bosnia/Herzegovina was controlled by Austria.
Austria had annexed (taken by force) Bosnia in 1908, a move that was not popular with the Bosnian people.
Franz Ferdinand decided to visit Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to make an inspection of the Austro-Hungarian troops there.
The inspection was scheduled for 28th June 1914.
It was planned that Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie would be met at the station and taken by car to the City Hall where they would have lunch before going to inspect the troops.
A Serbian terrorist group, called The Black Hand, had decided that the Archduke should be assassinated and the planned visit provided the ideal opportunity.
seven young men who had been trained in bomb throwing and marksmanship were stationed along the route that Franz Ferdinand's car would follow from the City Hall to the inspection.
The first two terrorists were unable to throw their grenades because the streets were too crowded and the car was travelling quite fast.
The third terrorist, a young man called Cabrinovic, threw a grenade which exploded under the car following that of the Archduke.
Although the Archduke and his wife were unhurt, some of his attendants were injured and had to be taken to hospital.
After lunch at the City Hall, Franz Ferdinand insisted on visiting the injured attendants in hospital.
However, on the way to the hospital the driver took a wrong turn.
Realising his mistake he stopped the car and began to reverse.
Another terrorist, named Gavrilo Princip, stepped forward and fired two shots.
The first hit the pregnant Sophia in the stomach, she died almost instantly.
The second shot hit the Archduke in the neck.
He died a short while later.

Gavrilo Princip was not executed because he was under 20 years, but was sentenced to twenty years in 
prison.
He died of TB (tuberculosis) in 1918.
The Schlieffen Plan was a military strategy created by Germany during World War I.
The plan was devised by Field Marshal Alfred von Schlieffen, who was in command of the German Army.
Germany aimed to avoid fighting a war on two fronts, so they developed a plan to swiftly defeat France before Russia could join the conflict.
The plan involved invading France through Belgium, despite Belgium being a neutral country.
This decision prompted Britain to enter the war in defense of Belgium.
Germany hoped to win the war within six weeks.
However, the plan did not unfold as expected.
The French and British forces launched a counterattack at the Battle of the Marne and pushed the Germans back.
This led to a prolonged and brutal war of attrition, with soldiers fighting in trenches.

The Schlieffen Plan was created to give Germany the best chance of winning in World War I. Germany believed that if they could quickly defeat France, they could then concentrate all their forces on Russia.
They believed that Russia would take longer to mobilize its army.
Germany planned to enter France through Belgium, which they thought would be an easier route.
However, the plan failed because the Belgian army resisted strongly, giving Britain and France time to mobilize their forces.
Germany also underestimated the strength of the French and Russian armies.
The plan was intended to result in a swift victory, but instead, the war became a long and bloody stalemate.
The Schlieffen Plan was an important part of World War I, but it ultimately failed to achieve its goals.
Germany's attempt to quickly defeat France and avoid a two-front war did not go as planned.
The plan was based on overconfidence and underestimation of the enemy.
The war turned into a long and brutal conflict, with soldiers fighting in trenches for years.
The Schlieffen Plan serves as a reminder that even the best-laid plans can go wrong in war.
It is important to carefully consider all factors and not underestimate the strength of the enemy.
The trenches of World War I were a brutal and unforgiving environment.
Soldiers lived in cramped, muddy ditches, constantly under threat of enemy fire.
Their lives were a monotonous cycle of digging, fighting, and trying to stay alive.
Life in the trenches was a constant struggle against the elements.
The trenches were often filled with mud and water, making it difficult to move around.
Soldiers slept in cramped, damp dugouts, often sharing a space with several other men.
They were constantly exposed to the cold, rain, and snow, and their clothes were often soaked and muddy.
Food was scarce and often consisted of hardtack biscuits, canned meat, and tea.
The constant threat of enemy fire made life in the trenches a terrifying experience.
Soldiers were constantly on edge, knowing that they could be killed at any moment.
They spent their days digging trenches, repairing fortifications, and preparing for attacks.
They also had to be vigilant for enemy snipers and patrols.
One of the most common injuries in trench warfare was trench foot.
This condition was caused by prolonged exposure to cold, wet conditions.
The feet would become numb, swollen, and painful, and in severe cases, could lead to gangrene and amputation.
Rats were a constant problem in the trenches.
They were attracted by the food and garbage, and they would often bite soldiers at night.
Lice were also a problem, and they could spread diseases such as typhus.
Soldiers would often use kerosene and other chemicals to try to kill the lice.
The weapons used in trench warfare were often brutal and deadly.
Machine guns, artillery, and poison gas were all used extensively.
Machine guns were particularly effective at mowing down enemy soldiers, and artillery could bombard enemy positions with devastating effect.
Poison gas was a particularly horrific weapon, and it could cause severe burns, blindness, and death.
The routines and strategies of trench warfare were designed to minimize casualties and maximize the effectiveness of attacks.
Soldiers would often spend days or weeks in the trenches, waiting for an opportunity to attack.
When an attack was launched, it would often be a coordinated effort involving infantry, artillery, and machine guns.
The goal was to overwhelm the enemy defenses and capture their trenches.
During World War I, transportation and weapons technology developed rapidly.
The result was a war with more casualties than had ever been experienced before.
During World War I, bigger field guns and cannon were developed.
Germany's "Big Bertha'' artillery could arch shells almost 25 kilometers upward to hit targets up to 120 kilometres away!
Giant guns were moved into position on railcars, and worked together in groups called batteries Often the guns fired shells filled with explosives and shrapnel, metal balls or fragments.
Germany used dirigibles, inflatable airships, for scouting and bombing missions.
Ferdinand von Zeppelin built huge rigid dirigibles by covering a light framework of wood or metal with a thin "skin" of waterproof fabric or aluminum.
The shell was filled with a lighter-than-air gas such as hydrogen, and the airship was propelled forward by an engine suspended underneath.
Britain used smaller frameless dirigibles to protect ships from submarines.
At first, fighter planes were used to find the enemy; later they were used to attack.

There was always a risk that the machine guns used to fire on the enemy would chop off the plane's own wooden propeller, so engineers developed an interrupter system to block the machine gun from firing at the moment the propeller passed in front of it.
This safeguard reduced the number of bullets shot, so many pilots used a top-mounted gun that fired above the propeller.
Both sides used poison gas during World War I. Germany was the first to use chemical warfare, releasing clouds of chlorine gas at Ypres in 1915.
The gas burned the skin and lungs of the Allied forces, including Canadians.
Later, both sides used phosgene gas (invisible but suffocating) and mustard gas (which creates huge skin blisters).
One young soldier temporarily blinded in a British gas attack in 1918 was Adolf Hitler, late he led Germany in World War II.
As the use of poisonous gas increased, troops were issued with anti-gas respirators.
Although the United States and Britain were responsible for much of the development of the early submarine, Germany used them most.

Their U boats (from Unterseeboot, or "under 
sea boat") used diesel engines and traveled faster on the surface than most ships.
A periscope allowed crew members to view the surface from underwater.
U-boat crews sank many Allied ships with torpedoes, cigar shaped bombs driven by a propeller.
The British developed tanks to crush barbed wire and shelter the crew from gunfire while crossing no man's land.
Soldiers would follow a wide line of tanks as the tracked vehicles crawled slowly forward.
The original tanks were underpowered and very hard to turn.
They also often get stuck in the mud.
By 1917, though, improvements made them important in the Allied ground war.
The Royal Canadian Navy (RCN) was established in 1910, following years of debate within the British Empire about the role of its Dominions in defense and foreign relations .
The growing naval arms race with Germany fueled this discussion, leading Canada to choose the formation of its own navy, which could support the Royal Navy if necessary .
The RCN, however, was in its infancy when World War I erupted in 1914, with only two obsolete cruisers, HMCS Rainbow and HMCS Niobe, and fewer than 350 sailors .
Canada's coastal protection was largely entrusted to the Royal Navy, which was occupied with locating and fighting German squadrons, leaving Canada vulnerable .
The perceived threat of German warships on Canada's west coast prompted the purchase of two submarines from the United States, which patrolled the coasts during the war, but never saw action .
To compensate for the shortage of Canadian warships, patriotic citizens loaned or donated their personal yachts to the navy, and the Imperial Munitions Board built additional vessels .
By the end of the war, over 100 small vessels had been pressed into service, mostly based in Halifax .
The Canadian Merchant Navy played a crucial role in the Allied victory, transporting troops and vital supplies from North America to Europe .

These vessels acted as a lifeline for the troops fighting overseas, as the United Kingdom was operating at full capacity and needed to import food, munitions, oil, and other goods to sustain the war effort .
The German U-boat threat posed a significant challenge to the Allied Navy, as these submarines could silently attack merchant ships carrying essential supplies .
To counter this threat, the Allies implemented a convoy system, grouping merchant ships together and escorting them across the ocean with warships for protection .
These trans-Atlantic convoys, sometimes consisting of over 60 ships, routinely made the journey from Eastern Canada to European ports .
The Canadian Merchant Navy faced heavy losses due to German submarine attacks, highlighting the sacrifices made by Canadian sailors who risked their lives to support the war effort .
The Canadian Government Merchant Marine (CGMM) was established in early 1918 to strengthen the merchant fleet and ensure the continued flow of supplies to the Allies .
The CGMM ships were intended to cooperate with British shipping in supplying the necessities of war and, in peacetime, to transport Canadian goods abroad .
At the start of the war airplanes were used mostly for reconnaissance.
The pilots would look for, and report signs of troop movement from the other side.
Opposing pilots were in fact quite friendly and even waved at each other.
This attitude soon stopped.
Pilots began to bring up pistols and rifles and shoot at each other.
When they mounted machine guns, the first fighters were born.
The German air force had several advantages at first.
They had more airplanes than Britain and France combined.
They also developed more complex weapons.
One danger of firing a machine gun was that you might knock out your own propeller.
The German Fokker airplane had a machine gun timed so that the bullets would not hit the propeller blades.
The common strategy in air battles was the "dogfight" in which squadrons of planes would attack each other.
The objective in these "dogfights" was to attack the enemy from behind or come at him directly from the sun where he would be blinded.
There were no parachutes to save the unfortunate who were hit or had run out of ammunition.

.. 
Great aces such as Manfred Von Richthofen of Germany and Billy Bishop of Canada were a special breed of men.
On the ground they could be courteous and chivalrous, while in the air ruthlessly efficient.
They were also prepared to face death.
A French pilot, Charles Nungesser, suffered seventeen wounds which left him with one bad leg.
an artificial jaw and gold teeth.
He had to be lifted into his plane and flew it with only one leg.
Pilots did not suffer the mud of the trenches.
They had good food and clean beds, but they also had the highest death rate of any of the services.
The average lifespan of a flier in 1916 was only three weeks.
Air Aces were the "knights of the air" and the first heroes of war.
They were instantly recognized everywhere and always received special treatment.
- Many Canadians excelled as pilots.
By the end of the war almost one-third of the British air force were Canadians.

Besides Bishop, other Canadians who gained fame as fliers included Raymond Collishaw, William Barker, and Roy Brown, who, it is generally agreed, shot down Germany's "Red Baron", Manfred von Richthofen.
Before sophisticated bombing devices were developed pilots simply dropped the bombs over the side of the cockpit.
In 1914 the plane was used for reconnaissance, had a top speed of 75 miles per hour and carried no guns or bombs.
By the end of the war the best fighters could reach a speed of 175 miles an hour and the bombers could carry up to 3 tons of bombs.
A pilot was classified as an "ace" when he shot down 5 enemy aircraft.
Women and WWI women's lives were changed dramatically as a result of the First World War.
Thousands of women served overseas during the war as nurses, ambulance drivers, workers in clubs and canteens for soldiers on leave, and personnel in army offices.
Many nurses worked in dangerous field hospitals just behind the lines of trenches.
Others worked in base hospitals in France and Britain.
Some nurses lost their lives and some were decorated for bravery and awarded Red Cross medals.
The largest role played by women during the war, however, was replacing men who had gone overseas in essential jobs in factories and on farms at home.
Thirty thousand women worked in munitions factories, and thousands more worked for the government or worked on farms.
Yet, even in the face of labour shortages, it was sometimes difficult in the early years of the war for women to get jobs in factories.
Many labour unions fought hard against hiring women because they feared that women would take jobs away from men after the war.
When women did get jobs, they were often paid less than half what men earned doing the same job.
Women also provided the majority of the workers in the volunteer activities that were essential to Canada's successful war effort.
In communities across the country, members of the IODE (see Topic 2.8) and the Women's Institute collected money, knitted socks, and packaged parcels for soldiers serving overseas.
Other organizations included the Nextof-Kin Association, the YWCA, women's patriotic leagues, vacant lot garden clubs, the Red Cross, and the Women's Volunteer Army Division.
